nameStory: Purslane speedwell gets its name from its leaves, which resemble those of purslane - that succulent garden plant with thick, spoon-shaped foliage. The "speedwell" part comes from an old English blessing meaning "may you prosper" or "fare well on your journey," given to these plants because they were thought to bring good luck to travelers. It's a fitting name for a plant that has successfully journeyed around the world!
description: Purslane speedwell is a small annual herb that rarely grows taller than a foot, sprouting from a single taproot each spring. This modest plant produces upright stems topped with loose clusters of tiny white flowers, each bloom barely wider than a pencil eraser. Its leaves vary from narrow and linear to spoon-shaped, giving it that purslane-like appearance that earned its common name. Despite its delicate appearance, this hardy little speedwell thrives in disturbed soils and can pop up almost anywhere humans have been active.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers only 2-3 millimeters wide arranged in loose, terminal clusters. Each delicate bloom has four petals and appears almost translucent when backlit by sunlight.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Variable leaf shapes from narrow and linear to spoon-shaped, with smooth or slightly toothed edges. Lower leaves have short stalks (petioles) while upper leaves attach directly to the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect annual herb growing up to 30 centimeters (about 12 inches) tall from a single taproot. Stems feel somewhat succulent and break easily when bent.

idTips.label: Hairiness
idTips.description: May be completely smooth and hairless, or covered in tiny glandular hairs that feel slightly sticky to the touch - this varies by subspecies.

habitat: Look for purslane speedwell in disturbed areas like roadsides, parking lot edges, agricultural fields, and waste ground throughout New England. It thrives in compacted or poor soils where other plants struggle, often appearing in cracks in pavement or along gravel shoulders. This adaptable annual shows up wherever human activity has disrupted the natural plant community.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge, forming small rosettes of variable-shaped leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and produce their tiny white flowers in loose terminal clusters throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, with seeds developing and dispersing before the first hard frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - only seeds in the soil wait for spring germination.

funFact: This tiny speedwell is actually a native New Englander that has become such a successful world traveler it's now considered a weed on every continent except Antarctica - talk about a local success story gone global!
confusionNotes: The variable leaf shapes can make purslane speedwell tricky to identify at first glance, as it might be confused with other small speedwells. Look for the combination of tiny white flowers and the mix of leaf shapes on the same plant - narrow leaves up top, broader spoon-shaped ones below. Memory trick: "Purslane speedwell has a wardrobe change from bottom to top!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "purslane" speedwell, this plant is not related to true purslane (Portulaca oleracea), which is in a completely different plant family. The name similarity is purely based on leaf appearance - a good reminder that common names can be misleading when it comes to plant relationships.
compareHints: Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats. While American brooklime prefers wet areas and bird's-eye speedwell has bright blue flowers, purslane speedwell sticks to white blooms and dry, compacted soils. Its annual growth habit also distinguishes it from perennial speedwells like the mat-forming thyme-leaved speedwell.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
